Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I have the honour to introduce Secretary-General's first report on Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS implementation, which is being submitted simultaneously to both the Economic and Social Council and the UN General Assembly. That alone signals something important. SIDS are a priority for all of us, but priorities must be matched by progress, and this report is clear about where we stand. The report presents a mixed picture. There has been progress. More SIDS are adopting Disaster risk reduction strategies aligned with the Sendai Framework. 27 countries in 2024 compared with just 6 in 2015. Renewable energy capacity per capita grew by 10% in 2024. Youth representation in national parliaments continues to exceed the global average. Yet structural challenges remain deeply entrenched. SIDS lose more than half a point of their GDP to disasters each year, more than double the global average. Nearly half the population faces food insecurity. 1 in 5 young people is not in employment, education, or training. These challenges are compounded by limited statistical capacity and fragmented data systems, making it difficult not only to monitor progress, but also to identify gaps and target support where it is needed the most. We now have a solution to this, a monitoring and evaluation framework with 59 targets and 83 indicators endorsed by the General Assembly in December last year. For the first time, we can measure ABAS implementation with a common, rigorous standard. However, the framework reveals that one of the biggest obstacles to implementation remains the availability of data itself. Of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals, only 3 have data available for more than half of SIDS. For the remaining goals, data average coverage falls below 50%, and for many it falls below 40%. The gaps are particularly acute in areas that matter most to SIDS. On climate action, for example, fewer than 10% of SIDS have reported any data since 2015. Ladies and gentlemen, closing these gaps will require sustained commitment at all levels. 3 imperatives stand out. First, embed ABAS into national budgets and sector plans, not as a parallel reporting exercise, but as a core driver of decision-making. Awareness at the central level is growing. Operational uptake across ministries is not keeping pace. That gap must be closed. Second, invest urgently in data and statistics. Too many countries are constrained by outdated legal frameworks, weak institutional capacity, and fragmented data ecosystems. Third, strengthen UN system delivery for SIDS. The report calls for a more coordinated and effective UN response, with better alignment of expertise, financing, and capacity development support to countries in need. It also recommends an independent assessment of options, including a potential single SIDS-dedicated entity within the Secretariat, for consideration by the General Assembly. This report delivers a clear message: Progress is underway, but vulnerabilities remain acute. For the first time, we have a common framework to measure implementation, identify where support is needed the most, and this should drive action. The midterm review of ABAS is in 2029, 3 years from now. The window to accelerate implementation is narrowing. The evidence is before us. The mandate is clear. Excellencies, now let's deliver on our commitments. Thank you, Mr. President.

The Philippines and Peru are pleased to introduce the draft resolution entitled United Nations Interagency Task Force on the Prevention and Control of Noncommunicable Diseases. This important procedural resolution reaffirms the continued contribution of the task force in reducing the burden of noncommunicable diseases or NCDs, improving mental health, and advancing the health-related Sustainable Development Goals. The resolution reaffirms previous ECOSOC resolutions and recognizes the growing global burden of NCDs, mental health, and neurological conditions, which continue to impede sustainable development, disproportionately affect developing countries, and widen health inequities. It also takes note of the WHO Director-General's 2026 report, which highlights persistent inequalities in access to services, the rising mental health burden, particularly, particularly among young people, the importance of country-led multilateral action, gaps in integrating NCDs and mental health into UN country frameworks, and the task force's central role in coordinating technical support. Importantly, the report recognizes the task force as an example of the United Nations delivering as one. As the Secretary-General's UNAT initiative advances, strengthening mechanisms that already demonstrate effective interagency collaboration will be essential. In particular, the resolution calls the task force to continue to: Number 1, Support member states in translating global commitments for effective prevention and control of NCDs and promotion of mental health. Support the capacity of member states to strengthen regulatory, fiscal, and legal frameworks that promote favorable health outcomes for NCDs and mental health. Strengthen its engagement with UN Resident Coordinators and UN country themes, supporting the integration of NCDs and mental health into UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks. The resolution also calls upon donors and other stakeholders to mobilize human and financial resources for the programmatic work of the task force, including through the Health for Life Fund. In this regard, the Philippines is proud to serve on the steering committee of the Health for Life Fund, which continues to support country-led action on NCDs and mental health through sustainable financing, partnerships, and South-South and triangular cooperation. Addressing NCDs and promoting mental health remain national priorities, as reflected in reforms advanced through the Universal Healthcare Law, health access, food labeling policies, and the Health Promotion Framework Strategy for 2021 to 2030. Building on these efforts, this September 2026, the Philippines will host the 3rd International Dialogue on Sustainable Financing for NCDs and Mental Health. Mr. President, at a time when we are striving for a more effective and coherent United Nations, this resolution reminds us that coordination is not simply an aspiration; it is a necessity. It demonstrates that by working together across the UN system, we can better support Member States in addressing one of the defining health and development challenges of our time. We therefore look forward to Member States' and the Council's strong support for this important resolution. Thank you.

Distinguished delegates, at a time when progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals remains uneven, And when many countries face the combined pressure of debt, fiscal constraints, conflict, climate shocks, and growing inequalities, a fundamental question confronts the international community: How can economic governance better serve people and accelerate progress towards sustainable development? The report of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Rights before the Council addresses this question through the lens of economic, social, and cultural rights, and outlines efforts by our office to support member states in this regard. Its central message is simple: economic decisions are human rights decisions. Choices on taxation, public expenditure, debt, social protection, and development. determine whether people can enjoy their rights: the human rights to health, education, work, social security, an adequate standard of living, and their right to development. This is particularly relevant to the work of this Council. Across discussions on finance and financing for development, debt sustainability, and implementation of the 2030 Agenda, Member States are grappling with a common challenge: How to translate international commitments into tangible improvements in people's lives? The report argues that a human rights economy can help address this challenge by ensuring that economic policies are assessed not only by their contribution to growth, but also by their impact on inequality, inclusion, and the enjoyment of human rights. Importantly, the report. The fourth is about the implementation. During the reporting period, OHCHR expanded support to governments, parliamentaries, national human rights institutions, and other stakeholders seeking to integrate human rights into economic governance. This work includes practical assistance on human rights-based budgeting, taxation, fiscal policy analysis, expenditure tracking, budgeting, parliamentary oversight, debt governance, and climate finance. The report highlights practical examples from different regions. In Bangladesh, OHCHR supported work on progressive taxation and budget tagging for social protection. In the Republic of Congo, we worked with government institutions to integrate economic, social, and cultural rights standards into planning, budgeting, evaluation and audit processes. In The Gambia, Ghana, and Somalia, our support focused on strengthening parliamentary oversight of public finance. In Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, our assistance reinforced budget monitoring, transparency, and accountability. In Kenya and Senegal, OHCHR supported rights-based approaches to budgeting and debt governance. In the United Kingdom, OHCHR supported efforts in Scotland to integrate economic, social, and cultural rights into law, policy, and budgeting. The report also highlights the ESCR Knowledge Hub launched by the Office in October 2025. The Hub brings together practical tools, methodologies, and promising practices on human rights indicators, budget analysis, fiscal assessment, assessment and monitoring. Together with technical cooperation and peer learning, it can support Member States' move from political commitment to concrete implementation. Mr. Chair, these examples demonstrate that advancing economic, social and cultural rights is not only about policies. Rather, it is about strengthening institutions and their capacities to deliver, improving accountability Improving accountability and ensuring that public resources reach those most at risk of being left behind. At the same time, the High Commissioner identifies persistent challenges, including limited fiscal space, rising debt burdens, climate pressures, conflict, insufficient data, and capacity constraints. These realities make it even more important to integrate human rights standards in economic policymaking and public finance decisions. As ECOSOC works to accelerate implementation of the SDGs in the final years to 2030, the report offers a practical contribution to the Council's effort. It demonstrates how greater coherence between human rights, development, and economic policy can help translate commitments commitments into results. OHCHR stands ready to support Member States in these efforts. Together, we can ensure that economic policies contribute not only to growth, but also to greater equality, inclusion, and the realization of economic, social, and cultural rights for all. Thank you.

Thank you, Madam President— Mr. President, pardon me. We thank the ASG on Human Rights, Claudia Fuentes Julio, for her assessment. We read with interest the report of the United Nations High Commissioner on Human Rights on the promotion of economic, social, and cultural rights through the concept of the human rights economy. On the whole, we agree with the author's opinion about the fact that the full-fledged implementation of the aforementioned category of rights largely turns on the well-being of the economic situation in a state. However, we wish to share the following remarks. The main thrust of the report is placed on stamping out inequality within countries, while the profound systematic inequality between states at the global level is practically ignored. Measures proposed to implement the concept of the human rights economy are not differentiated based on level of development. So that means there's a covert shifting of equal responsibility for the implementation of economic, social, and cultural human rights rights onto all states without considering the historical context, including the legacy of colonialism. Thus, the authors are drawing their conclusions without taking into account Article 2 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights, which enshrines the principle of gradual implementation of commitments to the maximum extent based on existing resources. And it also imposes on the parties to this agreement the obligation to implement these aforementioned rights not only individually but also in the context of international assistance and cooperation, thus imposing the concept of the human rights economy without linking it to the genuine economic capacity of states and without requiring that that developed countries provide assistance to developing countries could run counter to the spirit and the letter of the Covenant. These factors should definitely be considered. I thank you for your, for your attention.
